title: Energy is about 7% of the US price basket, yet it made up a third of 3.7% inflation
body: On 14 October 2026 the US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that consumer prices in September were [3.7% higher than a year earlier](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_10142026.htm), but only 2.6% higher with food and energy left out. Both numbers come from the same consumer price index, a basket of about 80,000 prices checked every month, in which each category counts according to how much people spend on it. Shelter, the cost of housing, is over a third of the basket; energy is only about 7%. But energy prices rose 20.4% over the year, and gasoline 34.2%, so that small slice added roughly **1.3 percentage points**, about a third of the total, because a part’s push on inflation is its weight times its price change. The index without food and energy, often called core inflation, leaves out the prices that swing the most, to show the slower trend underneath. And since energy takes a bigger share of some households’ spending than others, those that spend more on it, by driving a lot for example, faced more inflation than the average this year.

slides.question: Of every dollar in the US consumer price basket, how many cents go on shelter, the cost of housing?
slides.explanation: About 35 cents. Food is about 14 and energy about 7. The weights come from what people spend, measured in surveys by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.

slides.alt: Animation on night blue: 3.7% and 2.6%, a paper receipt listing a basket of prices, a grid of 100 cents coloured for shelter, food, energy and the rest, bars of price rises with energy at 20.4%, energy’s push of 1.3 points in a stacked bar, and two households with different baskets.

slides.prompt: Change how much of your spending goes on energy and on food. Find a basket whose inflation reaches 5%.
slides.takeaway: At about 14% on energy, twice the average, the same prices give you 5%. The official 3.7% is for an average basket; yours depends on what you buy.

slides.heading: US price rises, September 2025 to September 2026
slides.note: 12-month changes, not seasonally adjusted. Source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics.

slides.heading: Why look at core inflation?
slides.text: Food and energy prices jump around the most, so the US Bureau of Labor Statistics also publishes an index without them, which many people follow to see the slower, underlying trend. Both numbers are real: 3.7% is how much more the average basket cost, and 2.6% is the trend beneath the energy jump.

slides.question: Energy is only about 7% of the US price basket. Why did it push inflation so much in the year to September 2026?
options: Its prices rose 20.4% in a year
slides.explanation: A part’s push is its weight times its price change: a small slice with a big rise, about 6 to 7% times 20.4%, adds roughly 1.3 points, about a third of the 3.7%.
